title: Love brought back from ash
hookLine: Lalita wins her war, then brings Kama, love, back from the ash
carry: kama, love, is one of life's four aims
tomorrow: five things she does with the universe, and one of them is hiding
last: THE NOOSE, THE GOAD, THE BOW.

cards: What happens to love after it's been burned to ash? In the old stories, Kama, the god of love, once aimed his flower arrows at Shiva in meditation. Shiva opened his third eye, and Kama was burned to nothing.
The story told alongside the Lalita Sahasranama picks up from there.
Tradition says something grew out of those ashes: a demon named Bhanda, who brought misery to the worlds until the gods offered themselves into a sacrificial fire and the goddess Lalita rose from it.
Then comes a war, and the hymn, mostly names, tells the war in names too.

teach.h: HER POWERS CUT DOWN BHANDA'S ARMY.
teach.b: Read a stretch slowly and the story moves under the names like a river under ice. In paraphrase: she delights in the courage of her powers as they cut down Bhanda's army.
She delights in the young goddess Bala, who strikes down Bhanda's sons. She glances at the face of Kameshvara, her consort, and from that glance Ganesha is formed.
She rejoices when Ganesha shatters the device the demons built to block her army.
Then the end: with Kameshvara's own weapon she burns Bhanda, and his city with him, and the gods praise her glory. A fine place to finish. But the hymn adds one more name, and it's the surprise.
She is the life-giving herb for Kama, who was burned by the fire of Shiva's eye.

After the battle, she brings love back. Hold that next to yesterday: Lalita carries the same sugarcane bow and flower arrows Kama carried. The hymn doesn't treat desire as an enemy to destroy forever.
What grew wrong out of the ash is defeated, and the one who was burned is restored. Many teachers read Bhanda as desire gone wrong. It fits something Hinduism says plainly.

teach.h: FOUR AIMS: DHARMA, ARTHA, KAMA, MOKSHA.
teach.b: The tradition names four aims of a human life: dharma, doing what's right; artha, a livelihood; kama, love and pleasure; and moksha, freedom.
Kama is on the list. Wanting itself isn't the enemy. The hymn won't let a war be the last word about her.

how: The story of Lalita's war with Bhanda is told in the Lalitopakhyana of the Brahmanda Purana, and devotees who recite the Lalita Sahasranama pass through the battle in a run of its names.

o: a war chant sung by Lalita's army before battle
a prayer asking Shiva to bring back Kama
a hymn of names that also tells the goddess's war

games.q: a war told in names: tap the pairs.
p: formed from a glance; breaks the device

s: the hymn ends the war with Bhanda's defeat and nothing after
one more name follows: she is the life-giving herb for Kama, burned by Shiva's eye.
in the story, Kama was burned by the fire of Shiva's eye
the hymn's name for her looks back to that fire.
Hindu tradition counts kama, love and pleasure, among the four aims of life
with dharma, artha and moksha. the hymn won't leave Kama as ash.

games.q: you're Lalita. Bhanda is gone and the gods are praising you. Kama, the god of love, is still ash from Shiva's eye. what do you do?
o: leave him as ash: desire started all of this.
make a new god to take his place.
games.why: the hymn calls her the life-giving herb for Kama, burned by the fire of Shiva's eye. after the war, she restores love.

practice: Bring to mind something in your life that once burned out, a friendship gone quiet, an old enthusiasm, a hope set down, and let it be there like ash after a fire.
Without forcing anything, ask what small part of it might still be alive: a memory, a name, one phone number.
If you pray, you can bring it before the goddess, or before God, in your own words; if you don't, let the question stay open.

wordCard.voice: The Lalita Sahasranama. A hymn of names that tells a war, and ends the war with Kama, love, brought back from ash.

orig.note: Sanskrit kāma: desire, love; also the name of the god of love, who carries a sugarcane bow and flower arrows.

carryVoice: Your line: kama, love, is one of life's four aims. She burned the demon and brought love back. See you tomorrow.
